title: Acute Headache Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing acute headache, recognising life-threatening causes, distinguishing common benign headaches from serious pathology, and supporting safe diagnosis and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, neuroimaging or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Meningitis or meningococcal septicaemia (fever, neck stiffness, petechial rash, altered consciousness).
Subarachnoid haemorrhage (thunderclap onset, worst headache of life, neck stiffness, vomiting).
Acute stroke or transient ischaemic attack (focal neurological deficit, speech change, facial droop).
Intracranial mass or space-occupying lesion (progressive headache, focal signs, vomiting, papilloedema).
Giant-cell arteritis or other vasculitis (age >50, jaw claudication, vision loss, systemic symptoms).
Acute glaucoma (eye pain, vision change, red eye, halos around lights).
Hypertensive emergency (severe hypertension with symptoms, end-organ damage).
Recent head injury or trauma risk.
items.importantLimitation: Absence of classic features does not exclude serious pathology. Some serious conditions present with subtle findings.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise onset, severity, pattern and associated features to guide diagnosis.

items.title: Headache pattern and characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; first ever headache vs. recurrent; time of onset and progression.
Severity: rate pain 0-10; worst headache of life?
Location: unilateral, bilateral, focal or generalised.
Quality: throbbing, pressure, sharp, dull, tightness.
Duration: minutes, hours, days; continuous or intermittent.
Triggers: trauma, stress, menstruation, foods, medication changes, recent infection.

items.title: Associated symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, neck stiffness, rash or signs of infection.
Vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia or visual aura.
Focal neurological symptoms: weakness, numbness, speech change, vision loss.
Altered consciousness, confusion or behaviour change.
Recent head injury, trauma or fall.
Recent lumbar puncture or epidural.
Eye pain, red eye, vision change or halos around lights.

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Age >50 with new-onset headache (consider giant-cell arteritis).
Thunderclap onset or worst headache of life (SAH).
Fever with neck stiffness or petechial rash (meningitis).
Progressive headache or change in headache pattern.
Headache with focal neurological signs (stroke).
Known malignancy with new headache or neurological symptoms.
Immunosuppression with new headache and fever.
Recent anticoagulation or bleeding disorder with head injury.

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive features should trigger urgent investigation or emergency referral.

items.title: Meningitis or meningococcal septicaemia
urgentFeatures: Fever with acute headache and neck stiffness.
Petechial or purpuric rash (non-blanching).
Altered consciousness, confusion or seizure.
Positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign.
implications: Immediate hospital referral; consider empiric antibiotics before transfer if delay expected.

items.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
urgentFeatures: Sudden onset severe headache (thunderclap); described as worst headache of life.
Neck stiffness, photophobia or vomiting.
Focal neurological signs or altered consciousness.
Recent anticoagulation or bleeding disorder.
implications: Immediate emergency referral for CT head and neurosurgical assessment.

items.title: Acute stroke or TIA
urgentFeatures: Acute onset focal neurological deficit with headache.
Speech change, facial droop, arm/leg weakness or sensory loss.
Vision loss or visual field defect.
Ataxia, diplopia or other cerebellar signs.
implications: Immediate hospital referral for imaging and stroke assessment.

items.title: Giant-cell arteritis (age >50)
urgentFeatures: New-onset headache in person aged >50 with scalp tenderness.
Jaw claudication or tongue claudication.
Vision loss, amaurosis fugax or new visual symptoms.
Raised CRP/ESR or systemic symptoms (malaise, fever, weight loss).
implications: Urgent ESR/CRP; temporal artery biopsy may be indicated; consider empiric steroids if high suspicion.

items.title: Raised intracranial pressure or mass
urgentFeatures: Progressive headache or change in headache character.
Vomiting without nausea, especially morning vomiting.
Papilloedema, focal neurological signs or cognitive change.
Seizure, gait disturbance or coordination problems.
implications: Urgent CT or MRI head; possible neurosurgical referral.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examine for signs of serious pathology and focal neurological deficits.

items.title: General appearance and vital signs
howToTest: Assess consciousness, orientation and behaviour.
Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate.
Note rash, jaundice, signs of systemic illness.
normal: Alert and oriented, normal vital signs, no rash.
abnormal: Fever, altered consciousness, petechial/purpuric rash, hypertension.
implications: Fever with headache raises infection risk; altered consciousness requires urgent assessment.

items.title: Meningeal signs
howToTest: Test neck stiffness: passive flexion of the neck.
Kernig sign: flexion at hip and knee, then straighten knee (resistance = positive).
Brudzinski sign: passive neck flexion causes spontaneous hip flexion.
Note: absence of signs does not exclude meningitis.
normal: No neck stiffness, negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
abnormal: Neck stiffness, positive Kernig sign, positive Brudzinski sign.
implications: Meningeal signs suggest meningitis; urgent hospital referral.

items.title: Neurological examination
howToTest: Assess cranial nerves (pupils, eye movements, facial symmetry).
Motor: strength in arms and legs bilaterally.
Sensory: light touch, pain and proprioception.
Coordination: finger-nose, heel-shin test.
Gait: assess ability to walk, balance and coordination.
Reflexes: assess symmetry.
normal: No focal neurological deficit, symmetric strength and reflexes.
abnormal: Focal weakness, speech change, ataxia, pupil asymmetry or other focal signs.
implications: Focal deficit suggests stroke, mass or other serious pathology; urgent imaging needed.

items.title: Ophthalmological examination
howToTest: Visual acuity: test each eye.
Pupil response: size, equality, light reactivity.
Optic disc: examine for papilloedema.
Visual fields: confrontation testing.
Eye movements: smooth pursuit and saccades.
normal: Equal pupils, normal disc, intact visual fields and eye movements.
abnormal: Pupil asymmetry, papilloedema, visual field defect or eye movement restriction.
implications: Papilloedema suggests raised ICP; visual loss suggests vascular event or posterior circulation stroke.

items.title: Temporal artery examination (if age >50)
howToTest: Palpate temporal arteries bilaterally for tenderness, prominence, pulsation.
Assess for jaw claudication (pain with chewing).
Consider ESR/CRP if clinical suspicion high.
normal: Non-tender, palpable pulses, no jaw claudication.
abnormal: Tender artery, prominent or beaded artery, or positive jaw claudication.
implications: Temporal artery abnormalities suggest giant-cell arteritis; urgent ESR/CRP and consideration of biopsy.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports diagnosis but does not replace serious pathology screening.

items.title: Migraine
commonFindings: Nausea or vomiting; relief with rest and darkness.
Prodromal symptoms: mood change, fatigue or cravings.
implications: No urgent neuroimaging needed if typical history and normal examination.

items.title: Tension-type headache
commonFindings: No associated nausea, photophobia or phonophobia.
Triggered by stress, poor posture or muscle tension.
implications: Benign; reassurance, analgesia and stress management. No imaging needed if no red flags.

items.title: Post-infectious headache
commonFindings: Follows recent viral or bacterial infection (URTI, flu, COVID).
Associated with fever, cough or systemic symptoms.
implications: Self-limiting; supportive care. Investigate if symptoms persist or worsen.

items.title: Medication-related headache
commonFindings: Temporal relationship to new medication or dose increase.
Analgesia overuse headache: frequent analgesic use leading to rebound headache.
Nitrates, NSAIDs or hormonal contraception can trigger headache.
Improves with medication withdrawal or change.
implications: Review medications; consider alternative treatment if possible.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on red-flag assessment, examination findings and imaging where indicated.

items.title: Investigation
mustConfirmOrExclude: CT head: indicated if thunderclap onset, focal neurological signs, suspected SAH, raised ICP or recent head injury.
LP (lumbar puncture): if CT normal but high suspicion for meningitis (fever + neck stiffness).
ESR/CRP: if age >50 with new headache and constitutional symptoms (suspect GCA).
Consider MRI: if mass suspected, progressive headache or posterior circulation signs.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No red-flag features present.
Normal neurological examination.
Likely diagnosis is migraine, tension-type or post-infectious headache.
Reliable access to follow-up and escalation.

items.title: Refer or admit for hospital assessment
urgentFeatures: Thunderclap onset or worst headache of life.
Fever with neck stiffness (meningitis).
Focal neurological signs (stroke).
Age >50 with new headache and systemic symptoms (GCA).
Progressive headache or suspected raised ICP.
Altered consciousness or seizure.
implications: Same-day hospital assessment and urgent neuroimaging.

items.title: Acute headache
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: sudden severe headache (worst of your life), headache with fever and neck stiffness, headache with rash (especially non-blanching), focal weakness or speech change, vision loss, altered consciousness or seizure.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: headache with high fever (>38.5Â°C); new headache if age >50; progressive headache or change in pattern; headache with confusion or significant drowsiness; headache with facial droop or arm/leg weakness; or severe headache not responding to analgesia.

Speak to your GP if: you are having frequent headaches (more than 2 per week); headaches are interfering with daily life; you are using painkillers more than 2 days per week; or you want preventive advice.
